performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Marian Anderson takes the parent’s part in this song about the last looks of dying children, with Pierre Monteux and the San Francisco Symphony. A rising cello phrase becomes the voice’s first attempt to make sense of those eyes.

sections.label: A · A cello phrase becomes speech
sections.mNote: The contralto takes up the opening ascent

sections.label: B · The children’s wish, in D major
sections.mNote: Harp arpeggios and a vocal line marked warm

sections.label: A′ · The eyes grow distant
sections.mNote: Flute and low strings surround the returning phrases

sections.label: Coda · C minor after the stars
sections.mNote: A rising harp figure leaves the winds sustaining

cues.title: Cellos before the contralto
cues.text: The cellos’ upward phrase begins quietly and gathers winds and plucked strings around it. Anderson’s opening words inherit that climb. Mahler writes “Ruhig, nicht schleppend” — calm, without dragging.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, p. 18; our translation of Mahler’s marking. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A look understood too late
cues.text: “Doch ahnt’ ich nicht” — yet I did not suspect. Rückert’s parent remembers a brightness in the children’s eyes that now seems like a farewell. The poem is a sonnet, its fourteen lines ending far from the room, among the stars.
cues.evidence: Rückert, Nun seh’ ich wohl, German text at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text; our translation. The sonnet form is discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html

cues.title: A wish to stay
cues.text: Anderson now gives the children their imagined reply: they want to remain close. The harp opens into broad D-major arpeggios, with soft winds above. Mahler’s direction for the voice is simply “warm”.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 26–27, rehearsal 3; Rückert’s third stanza and the vocal marking warm.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The stars to come
cues.text: The reply ends with fate’s refusal. The flute carries a high, quiet line while viola and cello phrases move below Anderson’s voice. The last stanza turns the children’s eyes into stars shining on future nights.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 28–31, rehearsal 4 onwards; Rückert’s concluding stanza. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Winds after Anderson
cues.text: The harp rises after the contralto’s final phrase. Its chord takes an unexpected turn into C minor; flutes, clarinets and bassoon sustain while the strings fade. The score’s last instruction is “morendo” — dying away.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 32; our translation of morendo. Woltjer discusses the final harmonic turn: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: D major beneath “Leuchten”
transitions.from: A · A cello phrase becomes speech
transitions.to: B · The children’s wish, in D major
transitions.how: The voice holds back before “Leuchten” — shining. At Tempo I, the harp opens a D-major arpeggio above plucked D notes in cellos and basses. Flute, clarinet and bassoon sustain, and Anderson’s line broadens under the direction warm.

transitions.title: The wish meets its refusal
transitions.from: B · The children’s wish, in D major
transitions.how: D major darkens through A7 into G minor. The flute continues above the words about fate, with soft violas underneath. The cellos put bow to string after their plucked notes; horn and bassoon recall earlier phrases between the vocal sentences.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 27–28; Woltjer, song II, harmonic route through bars 44–60. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html

transitions.title: The harp turns towards C minor
transitions.to: Coda · C minor after the stars
transitions.how: After the voice, a rising harp figure outlines an A♭ seventh chord over plucked low strings. The expected D♭ resolution turns into C minor. The strings fall away, leaving flutes, clarinets and bassoon to sustain the final chord under morendo.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 32; Woltjer, song II, final cadence. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song II, printed pp. 18–32: the opening cello melody, D-major harp arpeggios at rehearsal 3 and the final C-minor chord.

timeline.note: The cellos begin alone with a rising phrase; winds and plucked strings join them.
Anderson takes up the cellos’ rising melody, surrounded by flute, clarinet and bassoon phrases.
Harp arpeggios open D major beneath the voice; cellos and basses pluck a low D.
Flute and violas sustain while bassoon and horn recall short phrases from the opening.
The harp rises into C minor; flutes, clarinets and bassoons hold the last chord.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
